clinicalPearls: Describes the metabolic and haemostatic derangements that follow replacement of a large fraction of the blood volume over a short period
The lethal triad of coagulopathy, hypothermia and acidosis compounds bleeding and worsens outcome
Dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy arises as clotting factors and platelets are diluted and consumed during massive haemorrhage
Citrate anticoagulant in stored components chelates calcium, producing hypocalcaemia that impairs coagulation and cardiac function
Potassium leaks from stored red cells and can cause hyperkalaemia, especially with rapid infusion of older units
Rapid infusion of cold components causes hypothermia, which itself impairs enzymatic clotting and platelet function
Major haemorrhage protocols emphasise balanced ratios of red cells, plasma and platelets, blood warming and correction of calcium
Frequent monitoring of coagulation, ionised calcium, potassium, temperature and acid-base status guides ongoing replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Massive transfusion syndrome is the constellation of disturbances that accompanies replacement of a large proportion of the circulating blood volume within hours. Coagulopathy develops through dilution and consumption of clotting factors and platelets, compounded by fibrinolysis and by the underlying tissue injury. Stored components are anticoagulated with citrate, which binds ionised calcium and can produce hypocalcaemia that impairs both coagulation and myocardial contractility. Progressive leakage of potassium from stored red cells may cause hyperkalaemia when large volumes are infused rapidly. Cold components lower core temperature, and the resulting hypothermia slows the enzymatic clotting cascade and platelet function. Tissue hypoperfusion generates a metabolic acidosis, and together hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy form a self-reinforcing lethal triad.
additionalDifferentials: Disseminated intravascular coagulation from the underlying injury
additionalInvestigations: Serial coagulation screen, fibrinogen and platelet count, or viscoelastic testing
Ionised calcium to detect citrate-induced hypocalcaemia
Serum potassium and continuous cardiac monitoring for hyperkalaemia
Arterial blood gas and lactate for acidosis and perfusion
Full blood count to track haemoglobin and platelets during resuscitation
redFlags: Diffuse microvascular oozing indicating established coagulopathy
Electrocardiographic changes or arrhythmia from hyperkalaemia or hypocalcaemia
Falling core temperature refractory to warming measures
Worsening metabolic acidosis with rising lactate despite resuscitation
reference.prognosis: Outcome is largely determined by the underlying cause of haemorrhage and the speed of control, but timely correction of coagulopathy, calcium, temperature and acidosis within a structured major haemorrhage protocol improves survival.
pitfalls: Transfusing red cells alone without proportionate plasma and platelets
Neglecting to warm rapidly infused blood and fluids
Overlooking citrate-induced hypocalcaemia during high-volume transfusion
Failing to monitor and correct potassium and acid-base disturbances
management: Manage within a structured major haemorrhage protocol with balanced component ratios to limit dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy
Warm the patient and all infused fluids and blood products to prevent hypothermia
Monitor and correct citrate-induced ionised hypocalcaemia with intravenous calcium
Monitor serum potassium with continuous cardiac monitoring and treat hyperkalaemia
Correct metabolic acidosis by restoring perfusion and controlling haemorrhage
Guide clotting-factor, platelet and fibrinogen replacement by coagulation and viscoelastic testing, with tranexamic acid where indicated
Achieve definitive control of the bleeding source
Coordinate haematology, transfusion and critical care management
